newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Holbrooke finds Bosnia vote largely trouble-free.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke finds Bosnia vote largely trouble-free.

text.p: The U.S. architect of Bosnia's peace treaty, Richard Holbrooke, pronounced elections held on Saturday to reunify the country largely trouble-free despite a Moslem claim of systematic fraud on Serb territory.

Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic's Moslem SDA party announced at the close of polling that it would not recognise Serb results. If the SDA (Party of Democratic Action) held its ground, efforts to form joint governing bodies based on the vote would be jeopardised.

Western organisers of the elections seemed unperturbed by the SDA manoeuvre. Some analysts regarded it as a bid to discredit Serbs in a post-election tussle for power and perhaps prolong U.N. sanctions against them.
Holbrooke, former U.S. assistant secretary of state, led an American delegation on a tour of polling stations on both Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic terrain.
The author of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty said his group had surveyed "20 to 30" of the 4,400 balloting centres.

"So we don't have definitive judgments. We have anecdotal evidence. What we saw was by and large an election in which we did not see things that would in and of themselves disqualify the electoral process," said Holbrooke.
"With one exception, we saw a trouble-free election," he told a news conference in the Bosnian capital Sarajevo.
Holbrooke described the SDA's claim as "very vague in nature" and said it would be handled shortly by international organisers of the elections.
Preliminary voting results were not due until Monday.
Holbrooke said he would go to Belgrade on Sunday with John Kornblum, his U.S. State Department successor, for talks with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on post-election steps in Bosnia.
Holbrooke and Kornblum will return to Sarajevo later on Sunday to see Izetbegovic.

Kornblum plans to go back to Belgrade on his own on Sunday night while Holbrooke will travel to Brussels to brief NATO commanders before returning to the United States to report to President Bill Clinton and the U.S. Congress.
"We consider the elections today the moment to launch a new intensive round of diplomatic activity," said Holbrooke.

Robert Frowick, chief of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's Bosnia mission which organised the elections, said the first post-war exercise in democracy in the country was "almost entirely free of abuse".
Regarding the SDA complaint, Frowick told reporters: "All parties came into these elections knowing that conditions would not be perfect."
He said he was surprised by the SDA's move but added that it would be dealt with by the OSCE's electional appeals subcommission in a ruling within 72 hours.

William Montgomery, special adviser to Clinton and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Bosnia, said the only serious abuse spotted in the tour of polling stations was in a Serb district near Gorazde.
He said Serb election authorities in the town of Kopaci "used a variety of tactics to frustrate the efforts" of Moslem refugees coming from Gorazde to vote where they once lived.

"These tactics included not opening one of the two polling stations reserved for these voters until the afternoon, slowing down the whole election process so the number of people who could vote at one time was very small, and refusing to allow 15- 20 percent of potential voters to vote," said Montgomery.
OSCE supervisors tried in vain to intervene. "As a result, many hundreds of potential voters from Gorazde could not vote, they were kept waiting eight-nine-10 hours."
